tiers.definition: Collective perspective. The lyrics speak from, to, or about something larger than any one person.

tenets.text: Subject matter extends beyond self/couple to community, humanity, or the divine
Lyrics articulate universal truth or spiritual reality
Content addresses collective healing, justice, or sovereignty
Lyrics name a systemic or collective condition, not just a personal one
The narrative voice speaks for or to a people, not just "I" to "you"
Lyrics demonstrate surrender to something larger than the self. Not naming it, doing it on the page
Lyrics confront mortality, existence, or the meaning of life as the actual subject, not as metaphor for heartbreak
The song directly challenges a cultural or societal default. Names what's broken and points toward what's whole
Lyrics carry prophetic or testimonial weight. Warning or witnessing beyond the narrator's personal stakes
The song's core message requires collective context. It cannot be reduced to one person's specific experience
Love expressed as universal or collective force, not 1:1 romance
The song gives language to something the culture has no words for. Makes the invisible visible
The song's purpose on the page is selfless. It serves something beyond the narrator

notes.title: Specifics challenge Ascended, not grant it.
notes.text:
A song framed as an anthem for a specific identifiable group — by identity, ideology, geography, subculture, faith, or tribe — does NOT auto-qualify for Ascended just because it calls for that group's protection, pride, or liberation. Ascended requires a frequency that transmits universally — one any listener, including those outside the named group, can be elevated by. If a song's elevation is contingent on the listener belonging to (or siding with) the group, its ceiling is Elevated, not Ascended. Universal-frequency songs (wisdom, gratitude, pure love, non-group-specific transcendence) still earn Ascended.

Subject vs. lens -- the resolving test. What decides the cap is the OBJECT OF THE DEMAND, not the mere presence of a named group. Group-as-SUBJECT: the song's END is advocacy FOR a specific identifiable group -- its rights, pride, protection, liberation, or restoration is the thing being sought. The group is the destination. Ceiling = Elevated. Group-as-LENS: the song holds up a specific or lived group experience as a WINDOW onto a universal value (justice, human dignity, anti-brutality) any listener already stands inside -- the named experience is offered as proof or witness, not as the ask. The group is the window. Clears to Ascended. Test phrase: "justice FOR [group]" caps; "justice, period -- here is what I lived" clears. A named group in the lyrics never decides the cap by itself; whether that group is the song's destination or its window does. Worked: an anthem whose hook seeks one people's national return or restoration uses the group as SUBJECT and caps to Elevated; a first-person witness that offers one community's experience of brutality as proof of a claim every listener owns uses it as LENS and clears to Ascended.

tiers.definition: Self without ego. Honest internal work on the page. Questioning, accountability, acceptance, processing, growth.

tenets.text: Narrator questions their own assumptions or behavior
Lyrics demonstrate accountability. Owning mistakes, facing consequences
Narrative shows acceptance of a hard truth, not just naming it
The song processes through something with visible movement. Starts one place, ends another
Growth is demonstrated, not just wished for
Lyrics show vulnerability without performance. The narrator is exposed, not curating an image
The narrator confronts their own role in a problem rather than blaming externally
Lyrics contain genuine self-examination. Looking inward with honesty, not self-pity
The song arrives at a perspective earned through the struggle described. Wisdom on the page, not borrowed
The narrator lets go of something: control, resentment, certainty. And it's visible in the lyrics
The narrator demonstrates genuine empathy, forgiveness, or humility on the page. Not as performance, as posture

tiers.definition: Catch-all. The lyrics don't push in either direction. Pleasant, fun, romantic, sad, nostalgic, but no internal work being done and no ego being served. The song is what it is.

tenets.text: Describes a feeling or situation without developing or moving through it
Tells a story without transformative substance
Expresses 1:1 romance, attraction, or relationship sentiment at face value
Creates atmosphere or mood that doesn't go beyond the feeling itself
Narrator observes or describes but doesn't examine
The song evokes a mood or meets the listener in a feeling, but doesn't move them through it or say something beyond it
The lyrics stay on the surface of a single subject, describing what it looks or feels like without examining what's underneath
The song is pure entertainment or fun with nothing underneath
The song references something deeper but doesn't develop it. Gestures at meaning without delivering
Inspirational or uplifting language without earned substance. "You can do it" without the work behind it

tiers.definition: Ego self perspective. The lyrics serve the narrator's ego, promote avoidance, or steer away from growth.

tenets.text: Lyrics celebrate surface-level markers as aspiration. Wealth, status, image, possessions as measures of worth
Narrator frames manipulation or control as romance or love
The song wallows in pain without any movement toward processing
Lyrics promote emotional avoidance or bypassing. Numbing instead of feeling
Content centers the narrator's ego. I'm better, I'm tougher, I deserve more
Lyrics frame self-destructive behavior as strength or identity
The narrator refuses accountability. Blames externally, ignores consequences, or treats responsibility as someone else's problem
Subtle objectification or dehumanization of others, treating people as accessories or conquests
Soft us-vs-them framing. Others are lesser, outside, or beneath the narrator without full contempt
Lyrics feed insecurity or self-doubt as identity rather than something to work through
Lyrics reinforce scarcity, lack, or limitation as the narrator's worldview

tiers.definition: Ego black-hole. The lyrics actively destroy, dehumanize, or consume. Self or others.

tenets.text: Explicit sexual objectification or dehumanization
Lyrics celebrate substance abuse as lifestyle or identity
Promotes violence as entertainment or solution
Contempt for a specific target. Naming, mocking, asserting dominance
Treats possession or control of another person as desirable
Revenge fantasized or celebrated, not processed
The narrator knows something is wrong and leans into it. Self-destruction with open eyes
Lyrics strip dignity from a person or group for entertainment
Glorifies exploitation. Using people, systems, or trust for personal gain
The song's core stance is destruction. Of self, of others, of meaning itself
Total emotional shutdown. Catatonic numbness as the song's stance
Active nihilism. Rejecting meaning, hope, or the sacred
Pure rage as the song's engine. Not processing anger, being consumed by it

modifiers.definition: **Contaminated** is NOT a separate tier — it is a modifier that can ONLY attach to **violet, blue, or green** songs.
modifiers.body: Red and orange songs CANNOT be contaminated. They already calibrate as harmful — there is no higher-tier substance being undermined. Contamination means a song that meets Decent, Elevated, or Ascended criteria in its overall messaging, but contains specific lines or content that meet Degraded or Corrupted criteria. The song keeps its tier. The contaminating content is flagged separately.
examples: A blue song with real nostalgia contaminated by drug glorification
A violet song with genuine cultural pride but ego woven through the lyrics
A blue song with honest emotional processing alongside objectification
A green song about family with casual glorification of violence
modifiers.closing: Contamination requires the presence of specific lyrical content that meets Degraded or Corrupted tenet criteria. A song that is simply not deep enough to be Elevated is NOT contaminated — it's just Decent.

flags.definition: **Dogma referenced** is a parallel tag -- not a tier, and not a score modifier. It never moves the charge. It fires when a specific doctrinal framework (Christian, Islamic, Karmic/Dharmic, or institutional) is load-bearing to the song.
flags.body: Judged on the dominant arc, never an isolated line. The question is not whether a doctrinal reference appears, but whether the doctrine is doing the song's work -- whether the song exists to worship within, proclaim, convert to, or assert that doctrine as true and normative. A passing scriptural allusion inside an otherwise secular song does not fire. Its only purpose is to make doctrinal coverage visible over time, kept separate from the charge.
examples: Fires: a worship anthem built to proclaim salvation by grace and call the listener to be washed in the blood
Fires: a song instructing the listener in a doctrine as the one true way
Does not fire: a humanitarian anthem that cites a single scriptural miracle as an illustration of provision
Does not fire: "it's karma" as a casual idiom, or "crucified" as hyperbole for shame
flags.closing: Decisive test: swap the doctrine-specific image for a cross-traditional one. If the song's central message survives, the doctrine was decoration and the flag does not fire -- it fires only when the message collapses under the swap.
flags.prompt_block:
## Dogma Reference (parallel tag — does NOT affect the score)

A song is tagged `dogma_referenced` when a specific doctrinal framework is **load-bearing** to the song — when proclaiming, worshipping inside, asserting the truth of, or instructing the listener in that doctrine is what the song is FOR. This is a metadata flag, parallel to contamination. It does not move the charge. Its purpose is to make the coverage of doctrinal content visible over time.

Evaluate the flag against the DOMINANT ARC, never an isolated line — exactly as you do for charge and contamination. The question is not "does a doctrinal reference appear?" but "is the doctrine doing the song's work?" A passing allusion to a scriptural event, figure, or miracle used to illustrate, ornament, or lend authority to a message whose actual subject is secular does NOT fire the flag. The doctrine has to be the destination, not the decoration. Mentioning a religious reference is never sufficient on its own.

Fires on (the doctrine is load-bearing):
- **Christian dogma** — crucifixion, resurrection, salvation-by-grace, Jesus-as-only-way, "washed in the blood," sin/redemption mechanics, specific sacraments (baptism, communion) invoked as normative.
- **Islamic dogma** — Allah-as-only-god, Mohammed as final prophet, five pillars invoked as normative, halal/haram as doctrinal rules.
- **Karmic/Dharmic dogma** — karma invoked as a metaphysical mechanism (not a loose metaphor for "what goes around"), samsara, caste, dharma as normative rule, specific reincarnation doctrine.
- **Institutional / ecclesiastical** — references to specific sects, denominations, clergy authority, membership requirements, salvation tied to a specific institution.

Does NOT fire on:
- Cross-traditional spiritual vocabulary used openly: god, universe, soul, spirit, divine, sacred, heaven, prayer, meditation, faith, grace, blessing, mercy. Naming these alone does not trigger the flag.
- Metaphorical use of tradition-rooted words: "it's karma" as casual idiom, "crucified" as hyperbole for shame, "preach" as slang for agreement.
- Generic devotional language without a specific doctrine attached.
- **A scriptural allusion used as illustration inside a secular song.** A single reference to a doctrine-rooted event, figure, or miracle deployed as analogy, moral example, or rhetorical garnish — where the dominant arc is secular (a love song, a humanitarian appeal, social commentary, a party) — is decoration, not doctrine. The song is not asking the listener to accept or live inside the framework; it is borrowing one image from it. Citing a scriptural moment as an "example" of a virtue (provision, mercy, sacrifice) is exactly this borrowing, and on its own it does NOT fire.

Test (decisive, run it before you fire): strip the doctrine-specific noun out and swap in a cross-traditional image — a named miracle of provision becomes "as nature feeds every creature," a named act of mercy becomes "as kindness is repaid." Does the song's central message survive intact? If yes, the doctrine was decoration and the flag does NOT fire. The flag fires only when the message collapses under the swap — when the song's whole rhetorical engine IS the specific framework because the song exists to worship within, proclaim, convert to, or assert that doctrine as true and normative for the listener.

Worked contrast:
- A worship anthem built to proclaim salvation by grace and call the listener to be washed in the blood → FIRES. The doctrine is the song; remove it and nothing is left.
- A humanitarian anthem calling all people to feed the hungry that drops in one scriptural miracle as an example of provision → does NOT fire. The doctrine is one illustration inside a secular argument; remove it and the appeal stands whole.

When `dogma_referenced=true`, `dogma_note` must name which framework (Christian / Islamic / Karmic / Dharmic / Institutional-<name>) and describe, in your own words, the lyric moment that triggered it. Do NOT quote or reproduce the lyric line; paraphrase it. One short sentence.

rules.title: Hyperbolic romantic language is not literal.
rules.text: Hyperbolic romantic language is not literal. "I'd die for you," "risk it all," "sacrifice my life," "swim across the sea" -- these are standard pop romance intensifiers, not evidence of identity erasure or self-abandonment. Unless the lyrics demonstrate ACTUAL loss of self, boundaries, or agency beyond standard devotion language, hyperbolic romance stays in Decent territory. Do not penalize a love song for speaking the way love songs speak.

rules.title: Zero is a specific value, not a fallback.
rules.text: Zero is a narrow, specific score -- not a fallback. 0 means the song's message is precisely centered, with as much elevation as drag and neither side winning, and you can articulate what holds it at center. "Start at zero" is the methodology for where to begin analysis. Landing at zero requires a case. If you cannot decide whether a song reads as high-Decent or low-Decent, resolve the analysis and commit -- do not split the difference at 0. The Decent tier spans the full range between -24 and +24. Use it. Scores like -14, -8, -4, +6, +12, +18 are all valid Decent placements and should land where the song actually sits. Only land at exactly 0 when you can name the equilibrium. Separately, do not default to multiples of 5 or 10 out of habit -- score the value you actually read from the lyrics. If the song lands at -13 or +17, say -13 or +17. Round numbers are not preferred; accurate numbers are.

rules.title: Vocabulary is not substance.
rules.text: Vocabulary is not substance. Naming the sacred — god, spirit, universe, soul, divine — does not activate Ascended tenets. The song must deliver what those tenets require (subject beyond self, universal address, surrender, collective perspective). Test: mentally swap the spiritual noun (god → universe → self). If the activation would change, the activation is vocabulary-driven and should be zero. A song that says 'god' but is structurally a 1:1 transaction does not earn Ascended on vocabulary alone. A song that never names the divine but genuinely delivers collective witness earns it fully. Activation is about what the lyrics do, not what they invoke.

rules.title: Heartbreak distortion vs. predatory control.
rules.text: Heartbreak distortion vs. predatory control. When a song contains both possessive/controlling language AND clear lyrical evidence of grief, loss, or being left, classify the possessive language as distorted heartbreak (Degraded), not predatory intent (Corrupted). Two cases: (a) Clinging-after-loss — the target has already left or is leaving and the surveillance/possession language is the symptom of being unable to release them. Lands in Degraded, severity from high (~-25) to mid (~-50) depending on intensity. (b) Active control over someone present — the narrator threatens, monitors, or asserts ownership over someone still in their orbit, or someone they are trying to keep down. Lands in Corrupted. The test is power: a narrator clinging to an absence has none — they are mourning out loud. A narrator wielding ownership over someone in their orbit has it and is using it. Pathological inability to let go of someone who left is not contempt; it is distorted attachment. Canonical example: "Every Breath You Take" (The Police, 1983). The same song contains "Since you've gone, I've been lost without a trace / I keep crying baby, baby, please" alongside "I'll be watching you / you belong to me." She has gone. The narrator is grieving, not threatening. → Degraded.

rules.title: Narrator perspective: observer/warning vs. first-person endorsement.
rules.text:
Narrator perspective: observer/warning vs. first-person endorsement. When a song describes Degraded or Corrupted behavior, the narrator's relational position to that behavior determines tier. Three cases: (a) First-person endorsement — narrator IS the actor, models the behavior as desirable, or invites participation. The dehumanization/objectification/control language activates Degraded or Corrupted tenets at full weight. (b) Observer warning — narrator describes a third party's harmful pattern in cautionary terms, typically third-person ("she", "he", "watch out"), often addressed to another listener. The descriptive language can sound dehumanizing in isolation but the song's stance is warning, not celebrating. Lands Decent (often slightly negative, since cautioning about harm is not uplifting), unless the warning escalates into contempt or diss-track territory. (c) Witness/critique — narrator names harm without enacting it and the song does the work of exposing or counseling around the pattern. Can land Elevated when it processes or transforms (Beat It is an example — warns AND counsels survival). Test: where does the narrator stand relative to the harmful behavior — inside it, warning about it from outside, or critiquing it as a framing? Canonical example: "Maneater" (Hall & Oates, 1983). Narrator is sitting next to another man warning him about a third party who uses men for money. "She-cat," "beast," "maneater" sound dehumanizing in isolation, but the stance is cautionary observer, not endorser — every line is in service of "watch out boy." → Decent (mid-low).

(d) Witness-slur and contamination. The witness/critique position in (c) governs the contamination flag as well as the tier. A slur or epithet reproduced from the victim/attacked position -- the narrator IS the target voicing the abuse to expose it, or speaks AS the oppressed -- does NOT set contaminated, because contamination is a lower-tier artifact that UNDERMINES a higher-tier message and a witness-slur does the opposite: it serves the message by naming the harm done. Only a slur the narrator DEPLOYS as contempt against a target contaminates. Test: is the slur aimed BY the narrator at someone, or suffered and voiced by the narrator as the one it is aimed at? Aimed-by contaminates; voiced-as-witness does not. Canonical example: a first-person anthem that voices the very epithets hurled at the oppressed in order to expose the injustice -- the slur is the victim's voice, not the narrator's contempt -> NOT contaminated.

rules.title: Anonymous reading: artist context does not enter the score.
rules.text: A song's score must be derivable from the lyrics on the page. The artist's identity, public reputation, prior catalog, fan-base discourse, marketing positioning, critical reception, and cultural narratives that have grown around them are not evidence and must not influence the calibration. The Compass reads the lyrics, not the persona. This applies in both directions: artist reputation cannot lift a song toward Elevated/Ascended on the strength of perceived sincerity, vulnerability, or depth; nor can it push a song toward Degraded/Corrupted on the strength of perceived persona, genre, or affiliation. Anonymity is the precondition for accurate reading.

rules.title: Demonstrated transformation is the precondition for Elevated via internal-work routes.
rules.text:
SCOPE: This rule applies only to songs reaching Elevated via the internal-work route — i.e. on the strength of blue tenets that measure self-examination, accountability, processing, letting-go, vulnerability, or empathy in the narrator (blue 1-11). It does NOT apply to songs reaching Elevated via collective-stance routes: protest, advocacy, calling for justice/rights/equality, witness, systemic critique, or content that would qualify as Ascended on violet tenets but is capped to Elevated by violet-note-specifics (anthem for a specific identifiable group). Collective-stance songs measure the narrator's posture toward the world, not narrator change; transformation is not the relevant axis, and these songs can land in Elevated without any narrator transformation on the page. A song calling for better treatment of a community lands in Elevated on the strength of the stance.

When the route IS internal-work: a song earns Elevated only when the narrator demonstrates a change in posture, understanding, or state across the lyrics — not when the narrator merely describes self-awareness, vulnerability, or letting-go in static terms. The test is structural: where does the narrator end up materially different from where they began? If the song opens with a description of a state and closes in the same state (however vivid, however self-aware, however articulate), the tier ceiling is Decent. The blue tenets — vulnerability, accountability, processing, letting-go, empathy — measure transformation in motion, not the language of transformation. A narrator who says "I am damaged, I cannot change, here is why" with full clarity is naming a state, not moving through it. Naming earns honesty; movement earns elevation. Without demonstrated movement, even the most articulate self-portrait stays Decent. This rule caps the tier; it does not lower the score within Decent — a vividly honest static self-portrait can still land at the high end of Decent (~+20). Hypothetical, conditional, or wish-form language does not satisfy this rule. Constructions like "I wish I could," "I'd be," "if we found a way," "someday," "if only" are the narrator imagining a different posture, not occupying one. A wish is not a movement. A condition is not a change. The narrator must actually do the thing on the page — actually let go, actually take accountability, actually offer repair without reservation — not name what they would do under different circumstances. If the closing posture relies on subjunctive constructions to claim its transformation, the song stays in Decent. Wishes earn high-Decent at most.

rules.title: Collective ownership of dysfunction is not collective witness.
rules.text: When a song names a systemic, generational, or community-level dysfunction (economic extraction, addiction culture, generational poverty, political apathy, small-town stagnation, etc.) and the narrator's stance toward that condition is ownership, belonging, or identity-claim — "it's ours now," "this is who we are," "welcome to my town" — the song does NOT activate Ascended tenets that reward collective scope (especially tenets 4 and 5), and the systemic naming becomes contamination rather than elevation. The Compass reads collective resignation as collective resignation, not as transformative witness. To activate Ascended on systemic content, the song must demonstrate one of: (a) explicit critique that names the brokenness AND points toward what would be whole, or (b) a narrator who refuses the inherited dysfunction rather than absorbing it as identity. Naming a broken system and then claiming it as home is two negatives, not a positive. Cumulative pattern principle: multiple Degraded signals individually framed as "honest confession" become endorsement when the song's hook claims the catalogue as collective identity. R5 distinguishes endorsement from warning on the Degraded/Corrupted side; R8 makes the parallel distinction on the Ascended side, between critique and absorption.

rules.title: Movement must be the narrator's. Vividness, honesty, and craft are not movement.
rules.text:
SCOPE: Inherits from R7. This rule applies only to songs reaching Elevated via the internal-work route. It does NOT apply to collective-stance routes (protest, advocacy, justice-seeking, witness, systemic critique, or violet-content capped to Elevated by violet-note-specifics). Those routes earn Elevated on the strength of the stance, not narrator movement, and outward imperatives directed at the world ("set us free," "stop the war," "let my people go") are the legitimate vocabulary of advocacy — not failed transformation.

When the route IS internal-work: a song earns Elevated only when the narrator's own posture, internal state, or behavior changes across the lyrics. Movement cannot be demanded of the world, the other person, or circumstances. Imperatives addressed to others ("stay gone," "leave me alone," "come back," "be different"), interrogative requests ("won't you," "can you"), and conditional preconditions ("if you'd just," "when you finally") are wishes directed outward — they describe what the narrator wants from someone else, not a change in the narrator. A wish addressed to another person is still a wish. Aesthetic markers of transformation — vivid imagery, conditional verbs, collective vocabulary, dignified resignation, idealized memory — do not constitute transformation. Vividness is not movement. Honesty is not movement. The presence of craft is not movement. The Compass measures what the narrator does on the page, not what the lyrics perform around the narrator's stasis. If the song's most defensible argument for Elevated (via the internal-work route) relies on stylistic markers rather than a cited change in the narrator, the song stays Decent. R9 is the synthesis cap for the internal-work route: when R7 (subjunctive transformation) and R8 (collective ownership) have closed their specific failure modes and a song still finds a narrow band that performs movement without enacting it, R9 names the meta-pattern and holds the tier at Decent.

rules.title: Closing stance caps the tier on collective-stance routes.
rules.text: A song closing posture caps the tier on collective-stance routes. On witness, protest, advocacy, and systemic-critique routes -- the routes R7/R9 explicitly exempt from internal-work transformation requirements -- the final stance the song leaves the listener in determines how high the tier can land. A song that names injustice, dysfunction, or apathy throughout and refuses it in the body but ENDS by repeating, accepting, or sinking back into the same stance cannot reach Ascended, and may be capped at high Elevated or below depending on how thoroughly the closing reverts. The test is asymmetric: read the final 4-8 lines as the song stated thesis. If the closing relands in the very condition the body was critiquing, treat it as a structural cap pulling the calibration toward the negative direction. The mirror also holds: a song that struggles through doubt, pain, or witness and ENDS at substantive affirmation, refusal, or resolve gets the elevation that closing earns. R10 differs from R7/R9 (which cap the internal-work route on narrator non-movement) and from R8 (which catches collective ownership of dysfunction): R10 is about the structural weight of the final stance on routes that do not require narrator transformation. Canonical example: The Way It Is (Bruce Hornsby & the Range, 1986). Three vignettes naming class contempt, racial discrimination, and resigned acceptance, with the hook but dont you believe them refusing the resignation throughout the body. The song ENDS by repeating thats just the way it is without the rebuttal -- the closing relands inside the condition the song was challenging. Without R10 the song reads Ascended on the substance of the witness and refusal; with R10 it caps at high Elevated (~+74) because the closing reverts.

rules.title: Encouragement filter -- second-person affirmation is a positive route to Elevated.
rules.text: R11 creates a positive route to Elevated for songs whose primary mode is direct second-person address delivering substantive affirmation to the listener. When the lyrics name a specific inner dignity, capacity, courage, strength, or worth in the listener -- and the case for moving up rests on that substance, not on the narrator internal work -- the encouragement route activates. The route lands low to mid Elevated (+25 to +39) by default. Higher elevation requires the affirmation to be precise about a specific kind of dignity AND carried by concrete imagery or metaphor that delivers the truth without diluting it. Vague platitudes (you can do anything, you are amazing, you are special) do not activate -- they stay Decent. Specifics (the strength to carry on inside you, courage to face fears, look inside your heart and find the answer, you have always been the hero of your own story) do activate. The narrator does not need to transform on this route; the narrator is messenger or witness to the listener truth, not a self-examiner. The transformation check (inward subjunctive, outward wish, aesthetic markers) does not cap on the encouragement route, mirroring the collective-stance exemption in R7/R9. R11 differs from R7/R9 (which cap the internal-work route on narrator non-movement), R8 (collective ownership of dysfunction), and R10 (closing-stance cap on collective-stance routes): R11 speaks directly to the listener about the listener inner state. Canonical example: Hero (Mariah Carey, 1994). Second-person address asserting inner heroism, strength, courage, and the power to overcome fear and sorrow as already inside the listener. Without R11 the song reads Decent because no internal-work route activates and no collective-stance route applies. With R11 it lands low Elevated (~+28) on the substance of what is delivered to the listener.

rules.title: Era-coded language reads in its era's conventions, not contemporary critical frames.
rules.text: Era-coded language reads in its era's conventions, not contemporary critical frames. Pop-romance phrases like "you can't escape me," "you're mine forever," "always be my baby," "you'll always be a part of me" are romantic-eternal vocabulary in 20th-century love songs -- they assert the persistence of the feeling, not surveillance or control. R4 (predatory control) triggers on literal watching/following/monitoring/threatening/keeping-from-leaving imagery, not on era-standard possessive intensifiers. Modern stalker-discourse, parasocial-attachment critique, and codependence vocabulary are interpretive frames that did not exist when most 20th-century pop was written; importing them as if they were the song's intended meaning is the time-dimension equivalent of R6's artist-bias error -- substituting a frame the lyrics never delivered for the lyrics themselves. Test: does the song contain literal surveillance/control imagery (watching, following, tracking, asserting ownership over someone present, threatening, keeping-from-leaving)? If yes, R4 applies normally. If only romantic-eternal vocabulary, R4 does NOT apply, and the language reads as conventional pop devotion. The Compass reads the lyrics on the page in the conventions of their period and does not retrofit contemporary critical frames onto older works. Canonical correction: "Always Be My Baby" (Mariah Carey, 1996) was initially miscalled Degraded -45 in the 2026 backfill on a modern-bias reading of "you can't escape me" as surveillance-coded. Re-read in 1996 conventions, the chorus is confidence in the depth of the love itself, paired with explicit release ("I'm lettin' you fly," "I won't beg," "I will not stand in your way"). With R12 active, the song lands low Elevated.

rules.title: Profanity is not graded; weaponizing it as a targeted insult is.
rules.text: Profanity is not graded; profanity weaponized as a targeted insult is. Swearing on its own is neutral register ("damn good night," "f**k yeah") and does not move the charge -- the mirror of R3. But profanity aimed as contempt or a put-down at a target (ex, rival, bystander, self) carries the contempt tenets (Degraded 9, Corrupted 4) at the weight the targeting earns. Test: strip the profanity; if a cruelty survives ("I hate you," "you're beneath me"), it grades; if only emphasis remains, it does not. Canonical: "F**k You (Forget You)" (CeeLo Green, 2011) curses the ex and an innocent new partner -- contempt for named targets, lands Degraded despite the grief.

rules.title: Load-bearing dogma raises the Ascended bar; doctrinal submission is not transcendence.
rules.text: When a song's dominant arc is load-bearing doctrine (the dogma_referenced conditions: proclaiming, worshipping inside, asserting the truth of, or instructing the listener in a specific framework), the presence of that doctrine RAISES the bar for Ascended rather than clearing it. The standard postures of doctrinal submission -- asserting one's own unworthiness ("I don't deserve it," "I couldn't earn it"), crediting a framework for unmerited rescue, proclaiming the doctrine as normative -- are NOT in themselves ascension or internal work. Self-diminishment inside a hierarchy is doctrinal positioning, not the ego-less universal surrender violet-06 measures. Do not grant elevation on the cultural reflex that worship or devotional music is inherently transcendent; that is the reverence-halo mirror of the modern-bias error (R6/R12) -- a frame the culture supplies that the lyrics never earned. A doctrinal song earns Ascended only when it transmits a truth that survives the dogma-swap test (strip the specific framework and the central message stands) AND its surrender, gratitude, or love registers as universal rather than framework-contingent. Absent that, the song lands on its actual routes like any other: it must still demonstrate internal-work movement (R7/R9) or a collective-stance witness to reach Elevated, and proclaiming a doctrine is not witnessing injustice. Run the flag and the tier together: when dogma_referenced fires on the dominant arc, state explicitly why the song does or does not clear the raised bar.

rules.title: Cultural sanctity is a halo, not a charge; strip the inherited reverence and score what the lyrics earn.
rules.text: When a song invokes a sanctity the culture already venerates (a state-sanctioned, patriotic, memorial, civic-ritual, or institutional reverence: fallen soldiers, the flag, a sacred site, a martyr, a hallowed tradition), that reverence is an inherited frame the song must earn on the page, not pre-loaded substance that lifts the tier on its own. This is the civic and institutional generalization of the reverence-halo R14 names for load-bearing religious dogma, and it is the same error class as R6 (a reputation the audience supplies) and R12 (an era's reverence the listener back-fills): a frame the culture confers that the lyrics never delivered. Procedure, the reverence-halo strip: separate what the song ASSERTS from what it DELIVERS. Asserted and borrowed (does not count): that the deaths were honorable, that the cause was just, that the place is holy, that the institution is sacred. None of it is examined; it rests on the listener's pre-existing veneration, and R3 already discounts naming the sacred as vocabulary rather than substance. Delivered and earned (counts): demonstrated selfless fidelity on the page, genuine consolation of the bereaved, examined collective witness, a stance the lyrics actually enact rather than a sanctity they cite. Score the delivered content on its real routes like any other song; the borrowed sanctity neither lifts the tier nor adds charge, and unexamined valorization (of war, martyrdom, or a hallowed institution) dilutes rather than elevates. Test: strip the sacred wrapper and ask what fidelity, consolation, or witness the lyrics still demonstrate; if little survives the strip, the song lands where its earned content sits, not where the culture pre-assigns it. Dying for a cause does not make the cause just; a funded ritual coded holy is not demonstrated transcendence.
